About this document


This document provides the teaching content for Earth and Space Science Years 12–13
of the New Zealand Curriculum. Equivalent for Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is being
published separately.

Progress and assessment information for Earth and Space Science Years 12–13 is
still in development. Once that is completed, Earth and Space Science Years 12–13
is proposed to be made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum
Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Earth and Space Science Years 12–13 will be required to start using it in
Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

Scientists develop meaningful questions and use experimental, modelling,
correlational, and classification investigations to gather evidence and explain
phenomena. They collect and analyse data, identify patterns and relationships,
evaluate evidence, consider alternative explanations, and distinguish between strong
and weak support for claims. Scientists test theories by attempting to falsify them
rather than prove them.
Investigating in science
Scientists develop meaningful questions and use investigations to explain
phenomena. They gather or select evidence (collect primary data or source
secondary data), analyse data, identify patterns and relationships, evaluate evidence,
consider alternative explanations, and distinguish between strong and weak support
for claims. Scientists test theories by attempting to falsify them rather than prove
them.
At Years 12 and 13, students continue to investigate scientific questions, gather and
analyse evidence, and use this evidence to explain scientific phenomena and develop
their understanding of Earth and Space Science.
Opportunities should be provided each year for students to undertake both practical
and secondary-source investigations, working independently and collaboratively.
Contexts and investigations may be selected or developed to reflect the needs and
interests of students, their community, and the local environment.
Delivery of Year 12 and 13 Earth and Space Science programme must align with
Safety and Science | Pūtaiao guidance.
Further guidance on programme design, investigation opportunities, and resource
selection is available in the Earth and Space Science Curriculum Support Document.

                                                                                                                                                   Geological timescales depict two important kinds of time,
                                                                                                                                                    relative and absolute.
                                                                                                                                                    o Relative time shows what happened and in what order.
                                                                                                                                                    o Absolute time indicates the number of years before the

                                                                                                                                                   Geologists represent large spans of time using units such
                                                                                                                                                    as Ga (billions of years) and Ma (millions of years).
                                                                                                                                                   The geological timescale spans the history of the planet
                                                                                                                                                    and is divided into different sections of time, such as eons,
                                                                                                                                                    eras, periods, and epochs.
                                                                                                                                                   Many of the divisions in geological time are defined by
                                                                                                                                                    changes in life, climate, and geology (e.g. formation of
                                                                                                                                                    oceans and atmosphere, Cambrian explosion of life,
                                                                                                                                                    breakup of Pangea, Quaternary glacial periods).
                                                                                                                                                   Radiometric dating is used to determine the numerical age
                                                                                                                                                    of rocks.
                                                                                                                                                   Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have the
                                                                                                                                                    same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
                                                                                                                                                   Radioactive isotopes are isotopes that have an unstable
                                                                                                                                                    nucleus, leading to radioactive decay at a specific rate
                                                                                                                                                    known as half-life.
                                                                                                                                                   Half-life is the time it takes for half of the unstable nuclei
                                                                                                                                                    (parent isotope) to decay into stable nuclei (daughter
                                                                                                                                                    isotope).
                                                                                                                                                   Different isotopes have different half-lives, meaning some
                                                                                                                                                    are more appropriate for dating particular rocks.
                                                                                                                                                   Geologists choose radiometric dating methods based on
                                                                                                                                                    the availability of an isotope and its half-life.
                                                                                                                                                   Geologists can use the proportion of the parent to daughter
                                                                                                                                                    isotope to determine an absolute age of a rock or fossil
                                                                                                                                                    (e.g. radiocarbon dating, luminescence, fission track, 𝐾𝐾/Ar
                                                                                                                                                    dating, U/Pb dating).
                                                                                                                                                   Other geological dating methods can be used for more
                                                                                                                                                    recent geological events (e.g. dendrochronology,
                                                                                                                                                    palynology, annular layers in ice cores).
